question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.
thinking: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX) is treated primarily with chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA; chenodiol), and adjunctively with lipid-lowering drugs such as statins. CDCA is a bile-acid ligand that agonizes the farnesoid X receptor (FXR/NR1H4) and (less potently) the G protein–coupled bile acid receptor TGR5 (GPBAR1); FXR activation induces small heterodimer partner (SHP/NR0B2), which suppresses bile acid synthesis enzymes including CYP7A1 and CYP8B1. Statins target HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) and affect LDL receptor (LDLR)–mediated cholesterol uptake. The causative gene in CTX is CYP27A1. Based on those drug–gene/protein relationships, the genes/proteins associated with drugs that can treat CTX are listed below.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cervical adenocarcinoma.
thinking: I interpreted the question as asking for genes/proteins that are molecular targets or clinically relevant biomarkers for drugs that can be used to treat cervical adenocarcinoma (including standard cytotoxic agents, anti-angiogenic and immune checkpoint therapies, and targeted agents used or studied in this disease). I listed proteins targeted by or closely associated with those drugs: pembrolizumab/nivolumab/cemiplimab -> PD-1 (PDCD1) and the PD-L1 biomarker (CD274); bevacizumab -> VEGFA; trastuzumab (used in HER2-positive cases) -> ERBB2; cetuximab (investigated) -> EGFR; paclitaxel/docetaxel -> beta-tubulin (TUBB); topotecan -> topoisomerase I (TOP1); 5-fluorouracil (sometimes used) -> thymidylate synthase (TYMS); and ipilimumab (investigated in combinations) -> CTLA4. I included these genes/proteins as the entities most directly associated with drugs used to treat cervical adenocarcinoma.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cervicofacial actinomycosis.
thinking: Cervicofacial actinomycosis is classically treated with beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillin, amoxicillin) and, when alternatives are needed, with tetracyclines (doxycycline), macrolides (erythromycin) or lincosamides (clindamycin). The principal molecular targets of these drugs are bacterial cell-wall transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) for beta-lactams and ribosomal RNAs/proteins for tetracyclines/macrolides/lincosamides. Below I list the standard gene/protein entities that correspond to those targets.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease chickenpox.
model_answer: Varicella-zoster virus DNA polymerase (DNA polymerase catalytic subunit, ORF28)
thinking: I treated “drug that can treat chickenpox (varicella)” to include the common antivirals used for VZV infection (acyclovir/valacyclovir, famciclovir/penciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir, brivudine). I listed the viral and host genes/proteins that these drugs are known to interact with or require for activation: viral thymidine kinase (activates nucleoside analog prodrugs) and the viral DNA polymerase (drug target) are the primary viral proteins; several cellular kinases carry out further phosphorylation of monophosphate nucleoside analogs (e.g., guanylate kinase, CMP/UMP kinase, deoxycytidine kinase, thymidine kinase 1) and nucleoside-diphosphate kinases that supply the final phosphate for the active triphosphate forms. Where possible I used standard gene/protein names and included common gene symbols.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cholecystitis.
model_answer: G protein-coupled bile acid receptor 1 (TGR5 / GPBAR1)
Apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT / SLC10A2)
thinking: Acute/chronic cholecystitis is treated medically with antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone, piperacillin–tazobactam, ampicillin–sulbactam, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, clindamycin, gentamicin), bile-acid therapy for gallstone disease (ursodeoxycholic acid/ursodiol), and symptomatic agents (opioids, NSAIDs). I listed protein/gene targets commonly associated with those drugs: bacterial targets of beta-lactams, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, macrolide/lincosamide/aminoglycoside binding sites, plus human targets of ursodeoxycholic acid and symptomatic analgesics/NSAIDs. This list gives likely proteins/genes associated with drugs used to treat cholecystitis.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cholestasis.
model_answer: SLC10A2 (Apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter, ASBT)
thinking: I interpreted “gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat cholestasis” as genes/proteins that are known drug targets or key bile-acid handling proteins affected by drugs used to treat cholestatic diseases (e.g., ursodeoxycholic acid, obeticholic acid, rifampicin, bile-acid sequestrants, ASBT inhibitors such as maralixibat/odevixibat, fibrates). For each gene/protein I list below I note the typical drug association: obeticholic acid → FXR (NR1H4); ASBT inhibitors (maralixibat, odevixibat) → SLC10A2; rifampicin (used for cholestatic pruritus) → PXR (NR1I2) and induction of CYP3A4; ursodeoxycholic acid and bile-acid handling → BSEP (ABCB11), MRP2 (ABCC2), NTCP (SLC10A1); fibrates (bezafibrate/fenofibrate) → PPARA; and enterohepatic transporters OSTα/OSTβ (SLC51A, SLC51B), OATP1B1 (SLCO1B1), and the phospholipid floppase MDR3 (ABCB4) are also central to cholestasis pathophysiology and are associated with drug effects. This list is my best-effort compilation of relevant genes/proteins.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease chordoid glioma of the third ventricle.
thinking: Chordoid glioma of the third ventricle is a rare tumor whose recurrent oncogenic alteration is PRKCA (D463H). There is no established, routinely used systemic drug specifically approved for chordoid glioma; primary treatment is surgical resection. Potential drug approaches that have been discussed or could be considered include inhibitors of protein kinase C (targeting PRKCA) and—by analogy to other gliomas—alkylating chemotherapy (temozolomide) whose activity is influenced by MGMT and mismatch-repair proteins, and combinations with PARP inhibitors. Because the question asks for gene/proteins associated with drugs that can treat (or plausibly treat) chordoid glioma, I list the genes/proteins most directly relevant to those drug strategies or to the known driver mutation.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease chorioretinitis .
thinking: I identified the common causes of chorioretinitis (notably ocular toxoplasmosis and viral causes such as CMV, HSV/VZV, plus bacterial causes like syphilis and TB), listed drugs used to treat these causes, and then listed the molecular targets (genes/proteins) that those drugs act on or require for activation. For antiparasitic therapy (toxoplasmosis): pyrimethamine and trimethoprim target dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR); sulfonamides target dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS); atovaquone targets the cytochrome bc1 complex cytochrome b; macrolides/clindamycin act on the 50S ribosomal peptidyl transferase/associated proteins. For viral causes (CMV/HSV): ganciclovir/valganciclovir are phosphorylated by CMV UL97 and inhibit CMV DNA polymerase UL54; foscarnet and cidofovir target viral DNA polymerase; acyclovir requires viral thymidine kinase and targets viral DNA polymerase. For bacterial causes: penicillins target penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs); antitubercular drugs target rpoB (rifampin), InhA/KatG (isoniazid activation and target), Emb proteins (ethambutol), gyrase (fluoroquinolones). Corticosteroids used adjunctively act via the glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1). The list below gives the gene/protein names (one per item).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified.
thinking: Drugs reported to treat chronic eosinophilic leukemia, NOS include targeted tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors (primarily imatinib), cytoreductive agents (e.g. hydroxyurea), interferon‑alpha, corticosteroids, and (in eosinophilic disorders/HES) anti‑IL‑5 therapy such as mepolizumab. I mapped each drug to its main known gene/protein targets or the proteins they act through (including relevant fusion proteins such as FIP1L1‑PDGFRA and BCR‑ABL1). The resulting list below includes those genes/proteins commonly cited as drug targets or mediators of these therapies.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease chronic eosinophilic leukemia.
thinking: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL) is often driven by tyrosine kinase fusion genes (most classically FIP1L1–PDGFRA) or other rearrangements (PDGFRB, FGFR1, PCM1–JAK2). Drugs used to treat CEL include tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib (effective for FIP1L1–PDGFRA and PDGFRB rearrangements; targets PDGFRA, PDGFRB, ABL1, KIT), FGFR inhibitors (for FGFR1-rearranged cases), and JAK inhibitors (for PCM1–JAK2 cases). Anti–IL‑5 therapy (e.g., mepolizumab) is used for eosinophil-driven disorders including some eosinophilic neoplasms. Based on these drug–disease associations, the relevant genes/proteins (including common fusion genes) are listed below.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease combined pituitary hormone deficiencies, genetic form.
thinking: Combined pituitary hormone deficiencies (genetic form) are treated by replacing the missing pituitary hormones or their downstream hormones/analogs. I listed genes/proteins that correspond to the hormones themselves, their primary receptors, or the proteins directly acted on by commonly used replacement drugs for the various pituitary hormone deficiencies (growth hormone, thyroid hormone, adrenal axis, vasopressin, and gonadal hormones).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease composite hemangioendothelioma.
thinking: Composite hemangioendothelioma is a rare vascular tumor with no large trials; reported/used drugs include mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus/everolimus), anti‑angiogenics and VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors (bevacizumab, pazopanib, sorafenib and similar TKIs), conventional cytotoxics used for vascular sarcomas (paclitaxel, vincristine, doxorubicin), interferon‑alpha, and occasionally propranolol. Below I list the gene/protein targets typically associated with those drugs (this is a best‑effort list based on published case reports and known drug targets; verify against primary sources for any specific case).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital combined immunodeficiency.
thinking: I looked for drugs used to treat congenital combined immunodeficiency (SCID) that have defined molecular targets. The primary drug-based therapies with defined gene/protein targets are enzyme replacement and gene therapies for ADA-deficient SCID (pegylated adenosine deaminase and the ex vivo ADA gene therapy Strimvelis) which target the ADA gene/protein, and experimental/clinical gene therapies for X‑linked SCID that target the IL2RG (common gamma chain) gene/protein. Other SCID treatments (hematopoietic stem cell transplant, IVIG, conditioning agents) are not specific to a single molecular target and therefore were not listed.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital factor VII deficiency.
thinking: Congenital factor VII deficiency is treated primarily with replacement therapies: recombinant activated factor VII (rFVIIa, eptacog alfa; NovoSeven) and plasma-derived concentrates such as prothrombin complex concentrates (PCC) or fresh frozen plasma. rFVIIa is the F7 gene product and acts by binding tissue factor (TF, encoded by F3) to activate downstream clotting factors (notably factor X and factor IX) and ultimately prothrombin (factor II). PCCs and plasma provide multiple coagulation factors, especially factors II, VII, IX and X. Based on the drugs used to treat the disease, the genes/proteins associated with those drugs are listed below.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital generalized lipodystrophy.
thinking: Congenital generalized lipodystrophy (CGL) is treated with recombinant leptin (metreleptin/r-metHuLeptin). The drug is recombinant human leptin (product of the LEP gene) and acts via the leptin receptor (LEPR). Downstream signaling involves JAK2/STAT3, but the primary drug-related gene/protein entities are leptin itself and the leptin receptor.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital hemangioma.
thinking: I identified drugs commonly used to treat congenital hemangioma (propranolol/timolol beta-blockers, sirolimus/rapamycin, systemic corticosteroids, vincristine, interferon-alpha, and anti-VEGF therapy like bevacizumab) and listed the primary gene/protein targets associated with those drugs according to standard gene/protein names.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
thinking: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is treated by replacing or stimulating the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal hormones. Common therapies and their molecular targets: pulsatile GnRH (native GNRH1 or synthetic GnRH) acts on the gonadotropin‑releasing hormone receptor (GNRHR); gonadotropin preparations (hCG, hMG, recombinant LH/FSH) act via the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR) and the follicle‑stimulating hormone receptor (FSHR) and are composed of or related to the gonadotropin subunit proteins (LHB, FSHB, CGA); testosterone replacement signals via the androgen receptor (AR). Kisspeptin and its receptor (KISS1, KISS1R) are also relevant because kisspeptin agonists can stimulate GnRH secretion and have been used experimentally in CHH. Based on these treatment–target relationships, the genes/proteins associated with drugs that can treat CHH are listed below.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital isolated hyperinsulinism.
thinking: Congenital isolated hyperinsulinism (congenital hyperinsulinism) is treated medically with drugs that act on pancreatic beta-cell KATP channels, somatostatin receptors, voltage-gated calcium channels, the glucagon receptor, or mTOR. Key drugs and their primary molecular targets: diazoxide (opens KATP channels composed of SUR1/ABCC8 and Kir6.2/KCNJ11), octreotide/lanreotide (somatostatin analogs acting mainly at SSTR2 and SSTR5), nifedipine (L-type voltage-gated calcium channels such as CACNA1C and CACNA1D), glucagon (glucagon receptor GCGR), and sirolimus/rapamycin (mTOR/MTOR). The list below gives the standard gene/protein names for those targets.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital prothrombin deficiency.
thinking: Congenital prothrombin deficiency is caused by lack of prothrombin (factor II, encoded by F2). Treatments reported in guidelines and case series include plasma-derived prothrombin complex concentrates (PCCs, 4‑factor PCCs), fresh frozen plasma, and sometimes recombinant activated factor VII (rFVIIa) or antifibrinolytics as adjuncts. 4‑factor PCCs contain coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X and also contain the natural anticoagulant proteins C and S; antifibrinolytic drugs (e.g., tranexamic acid) act on the plasminogen/plasmin system. Therefore the genes/proteins associated with drugs used to treat congenital prothrombin deficiency include: F2 (prothrombin), F7 (coagulation factor VII), F9 (coagulation factor IX), F10 (coagulation factor X), PROC (protein C), PROS1 (protein S), and PLG (plasminogen).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease congenital toxoplasmosis.
thinking: Congenital toxoplasmosis is treated clinically with combinations such as pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine (with folinic acid), spiramycin, clindamycin, atovaquone, and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Key drug targets in Toxoplasma gondii (and relevant microbial targets) include dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthase (targets of pyrimethamine/trimethoprim), dihydropteroate synthase (target of sulfonamides like sulfadiazine), cytochrome b (target of atovaquone), and apicoplast/50S ribosomal proteins (targets of macrolides/lincosamides such as spiramycin and clindamycin). The list below gives the standard protein/gene names for those targets.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease constitutional neutropenia.
thinking: Constitutional (benign) neutropenia is commonly treated when needed with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) preparations (e.g., filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, lenograstim) and sometimes with granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF, e.g., sargramostim). The primary drug proteins/genes are the ligands and their receptors; key downstream signaling proteins involved in G-CSF/GM-CSF signaling are also listed as they are molecularly associated with the drug action. Listed below are the standard gene/protein names associated with those drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease contagious pustular dermatitis.
thinking: Contagious pustular dermatitis (orf/contagious ecthyma) is usually self-limited but has been treated in humans and animals with topical antiviral or immune-modulating drugs. Reported therapeutics include imiquimod (a TLR7 agonist), topical or intralesional cidofovir (a cytosine nucleotide analog that inhibits viral DNA polymerases), interferon-alpha, and occasionally nucleoside antivirals (e.g., acyclovir) in some cases. I therefore list the main genes/proteins that are the known direct targets or primary host receptors through which those drugs act: TLR7 (imiquimod), (less strongly) TLR8, IFNAR1 and IFNAR2 (interferon-alpha receptor subunits), viral DNA polymerase (target of cidofovir), and viral thymidine kinase (activating/targeting enzyme for nucleoside antivirals such as acyclovir). There is uncertainty because many treatments are supportive and some drugs act indirectly via downstream signaling (MyD88, IRF7, JAK1/TYK2, STATs), which I did not list as primary drug targets.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease coronary artery disease.
thinking: I interpreted the request as: list genes/proteins that are molecularly associated with drugs used to treat coronary artery disease (CAD). I included primary drug targets (receptors, enzymes, ion channels), key transporters and enzymes that activate or metabolize those drugs, and major proteins directly acted on by anticoagulants/thrombolytics. The list covers major drug classes used in CAD (statins, PCSK9 inhibitors, ezetimibe, fibrates, antiplatelets, beta‑blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium‑channel blockers, nitrates/NO pathway, anticoagulants, thrombolytics, antianginal agents, and relevant drug‑metabolizing/transport proteins). This is not an exhaustive list of every possible minor interaction, but it captures the principal gene/protein associations for commonly used CAD drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cowpox.
thinking: Cowpox is an orthopoxvirus; the main antivirals used or investigated against orthopoxviruses (including cowpox) are tecovirimat (ST-246/TPOXX), which targets the viral VP37 envelope-wrapping protein encoded by the F13L gene, and cidofovir/brincidofovir (lipid prodrug CMX001), which inhibit the viral DNA polymerase encoded by E9L. Ribavirin has been used experimentally against some orthopoxviruses and acts primarily via inhibition of host inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH1/IMPDH2), though its efficacy for cowpox is limited. Based on known drug–target associations for agents used to treat or investigate treatment of cowpox, the relevant gene/protein entities are listed below.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease creeping myiasis.
model_answer: Voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit (para / NaV)
thinking: Creeping myiasis (cutaneous myiasis/larval infestations) is commonly treated with topical or oral ivermectin, topical permethrin, and benzimidazole anthelmintics (e.g., thiabendazole, albendazole) or mechanical removal. Ivermectin acts primarily on invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels and also modulates GABA-gated chloride channels; permethrin targets insect voltage-gated sodium channels; benzimidazoles bind parasite beta-tubulin. Host parasite-drug disposition is influenced by P-glycoprotein (ABCB1). Based on these drug–target relationships, the genes/proteins associated with drugs that can treat creeping myiasis include the glutamate-gated chloride channels (and specific subunits known from parasitic nematodes), GABA-gated chloride channels, voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit, beta-tubulin, and P-glycoprotein.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cryptococcosis.
thinking: I identified the antifungal drugs used to treat cryptococcosis (mainly azoles, amphotericin B, and flucytosine) and listed the fungal genes/proteins that are known drug targets or are commonly associated with drug action or resistance for those agents (azole target ERG11/CYP51; amphotericin B interacts with ergosterol and ergosterol-biosynthesis enzymes; flucytosine requires uptake/conversion by FCY2/FCY1 and acts via pathways involving FUR1; echinocandin target FKS1; efflux and tolerance mechanisms involve transporters and stress-response proteins such as AFR1, HSP90, calcineurin, etc.).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cryptosporidiosis.
thinking: I interpreted the question as asking for genes/proteins that are known or plausibly reported as targets (or drug-associated molecular entities) of drugs used to treat cryptosporidiosis (approved, commonly used, or in clinical/preclinical development). Key examples: nitazoxanide (the approved drug) is thought to interfere with pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR)-dependent metabolism; aminoglycosides and macrolides used empirically act on ribosomal RNA/proteins (30S/16S and 50S/23S, respectively); recent investigational compounds (bumped kinase inhibitors) target Cryptosporidium CDPK1; several preclinical antiprotozoal leads target aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (e.g., MetRS, PheRS) or nucleotide biosynthesis enzymes such as IMPDH. I included the canonical names of these genes/proteins as the best-available list of molecular entities associated with drugs that can treat or are being developed to treat cryptosporidiosis.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cutaneous larva migrans.
thinking: Cutaneous larva migrans is most commonly treated with benzimidazole anthelmintics (albendazole, mebendazole, thiabendazole) and with the macrocyclic lactone ivermectin. The primary parasite targets and parasite resistance-associated proteins for those drugs are well described: benzimidazoles bind parasite beta-tubulin (ben-1 and related beta-tubulin genes); ivermectin acts on glutamate-gated chloride channels (and can also affect GABA-gated chloride channels), and P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) is implicated in ivermectin transport/resistance. I also included commonly referenced specific parasite gene names and a major human hepatic enzyme (CYP3A4) known to metabolize albendazole, since metabolic enzymes are often associated with drug action. The list below gives the gene/protein entities associated with drugs used to treat cutaneous larva migrans.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma.
thinking: Cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma is most commonly Merkel cell carcinoma. Drugs used to treat it include immune checkpoint inhibitors (avelumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab, sometimes ipilimumab) and conventional chemotherapies (etoposide, platinum agents, anthracyclines, topotecan, vinca alkaloids, taxanes), plus occasional somatostatin analog use in neuroendocrine contexts. I listed the primary protein/gene targets of those drugs: PD-L1 (target of avelumab), PD-1 (target of pembrolizumab/nivolumab), CTLA-4 (ipilimumab), topoisomerase II alpha/beta (etoposide, doxorubicin), topoisomerase I (topotecan), beta tubulin (vinca alkaloids/taxanes), and somatostatin receptor 2 (somatostatin analogs). Some chemotherapies (platinum agents, cyclophosphamide) act by DNA damage or require metabolic activation rather than a single protein target, so they are not represented here. This list is based on typical treatments and their known molecular targets; exact drug use can vary clinically.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cyclic hematopoiesis.
thinking: Cyclic hematopoiesis (cyclic neutropenia) is treated with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G‑CSF) drugs such as filgrastim/pegfilgrastim. These drugs are recombinant G‑CSF (gene/protein CSF3) and act on the G‑CSF receptor (gene/protein CSF3R). Therefore the relevant gene/protein entities are CSF3 and CSF3R.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cystic echinococcosis.
model_answer: Voltage-gated (voltage-dependent) calcium channel alpha-1 subunit (CACNA1 family)
Transient receptor potential melastatin channel (TRPM family)
thinking: Cystic echinococcosis (hydatid disease) is treated primarily with benzimidazole drugs (albendazole, mebendazole), sometimes combined with praziquantel and less commonly other antiparasitics (nitazoxanide, etc.). Key parasite and host proteins associated with those drugs include the benzimidazole target (beta‑tubulin), parasite/host drug transporters and metabolizing enzymes that affect drug levels and resistance (P‑glycoprotein/ABCB1, CYP3A4), praziquantel’s likely parasite ion‑channel targets (voltage‑gated calcium channels and parasite TRP channels) and enzymes targeted by nitazoxanide (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase). I list the standard gene/protein names below (each entry is a single entity).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cysticercosis.
model_answer: Voltage-dependent calcium channel, alpha-1 subunit (CACNA1 family)
Transient receptor potential channel, M family (TRPM) — e.g., praziquantel-activated TRP channels (Sm.TRPM_PZQ type)
ATP synthase, mitochondrial (ATP5A1 and other ATP synthase subunits)
NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) / Complex I (ND genes and nuclear NDUF subunits)
thinking: Cysticercosis (Taenia solium infection) is treated primarily with antiparasitic drugs such as albendazole and praziquantel (also niclosamide and adjunctive agents are used). Known drug–protein associations: albendazole binds parasite beta-tubulin and disrupts microtubules; praziquantel acts via parasite calcium handling including activation of parasite TRP-type channels and effects on voltage-gated calcium channels; niclosamide disrupts parasite mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (complex I/fumarate reductase/ATP synthase). In humans these drugs are metabolized/transported by enzymes and transporters (noted here because they are commonly reported protein associations). The list below gives the main gene/protein entities associated with these antiparasitic drugs (targets and major metabolizing/transport proteins).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cystinosis.
thinking: Interpretation: the drug used to treat cystinosis is cysteamine (cysteamine bitartrate). Genes/proteins relevant to cystinosis treatment include the disease gene (CTNS, encoding the lysosomal cystine transporter cystinosin) and proteins involved in the cysteamine-dependent alternative cystine export/metabolism pathway. Based on literature knowledge, key associated genes/proteins are CTNS, the lysosomal PQ-loop transporter PQLC2 (also implicated in efflux of cysteine–cysteamine mixed disulfide), and the enzyme cysteamine dioxygenase (ADO), which metabolizes cysteamine. There is some uncertainty about additional transporters or enzymes that may also be involved, but the list below gives the primary, well-recognized associated genes/proteins.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cytomegalovirus infection.
thinking: I identified drugs used to treat cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection and their known molecular targets. Ganciclovir and valganciclovir are activated by the viral kinase UL97 and inhibit the viral DNA polymerase (UL54). Foscarnet and cidofovir directly inhibit the viral DNA polymerase (UL54). Maribavir targets the viral kinase UL97. Letermovir targets the viral terminase complex (principally UL56 and UL89). The antisense drug fomivirsen targets the CMV immediate-early mRNA encoding IE2 (UL122). Based on these drug–target relationships, the genes/proteins associated with drugs that can treat CMV infection are listed below.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease cytomegalovirus retinitis.
thinking: I identified drugs used to treat CMV retinitis (ganciclovir/valganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir, fomivirsen) and other anti-CMV agents relevant to CMV disease (maribavir, letermovir). I then listed the viral genes/proteins known to be associated with the mechanism of action or drug resistance for those drugs: UL97 (viral kinase activated ganciclovir and is inhibited by maribavir), UL54 (viral DNA polymerase targeted by ganciclovir, foscarnet and cidofovir), UL122 (major immediate-early protein IE2 targeted by the antisense drug fomivirsen), and the terminase complex subunits UL56 and UL89 targeted by letermovir. I also included UL123 (IE1) because the immediate-early transcripts/proteins (IE1/IE2) are the fomivirsen target region in CMV immediate-early mRNA.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease degeneration of macula and posterior pole.
thinking: I identified drugs used to treat degeneration of the macula and posterior pole (notably anti‑VEGF biologics for neovascular AMD and complement inhibitors for geographic atrophy). I listed the protein/gene targets of those drugs: anti‑VEGF agents target VEGF family members (VEGFA, VEGFB, PGF) and are functionally related to VEGF receptors (FLT1/VEGFR1 and KDR/VEGFR2); newer bispecifics also target ANGPT2. Complement inhibitors approved or in late‑stage use target complement components C3 and C5. I included the standard gene/protein names.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.
thinking: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is commonly driven by a COL1A1–PDGFB fusion that activates PDGFRB. The tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib is used to treat DFSP and its known molecular targets include PDGFRB (the primary relevant receptor), PDGFB (the fusion partner that drives PDGFRB activation), and COL1A1 (the fusion partner gene). Imatinib also targets other kinases clinically associated with the drug’s activity (ABL1 including the BCR-ABL fusion, KIT, and PDGFRA), so those genes/proteins are listed as well.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease diabetic cataract.
thinking: Primary pharmacologic approaches to preventing or slowing diabetic cataract focus on the polyol pathway and oxidative/AGE-related damage. Aldose reductase inhibitors (e.g., epalrestat, ranirestat, sorbinil) directly target aldose reductase (AKR1B1). The polyol pathway also involves sorbitol dehydrogenase (SORD). Drugs that reduce formation/effects of advanced glycation endproducts (e.g., aminoguanidine) act on AGE/RAGE-related processes (AGER). Antioxidant therapies are intended to modulate lens oxidative stress through enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD1), catalase (CAT) and glutathione peroxidase (GPX1). Some systemic glucose-lowering drugs like metformin have been associated epidemiologically with reduced cataract risk and act via AMPK (PRKAA1/PRKAA2). AKR1B10 is an additional aldo-keto reductase family member sometimes considered in this context. Surgical extraction remains the definitive treatment; the listed genes/proteins are those plausibly associated with drugs investigated for treating or preventing diabetic cataract (some associations are stronger/clearer than others).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease diabetic retinopathy.
thinking: Approved treatments for diabetic retinopathy include intravitreal anti‑VEGF agents (ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept, brolucizumab, pegaptanib, conbercept, faricimab) and intravitreal corticosteroids (triamcinolone, dexamethasone implant, fluocinolone). Anti‑VEGF drugs act on VEGF family members and their receptors (VEGFA is the primary target; aflibercept and conbercept bind VEGF-A/B and placental growth factor PGF; faricimab is bispecific for VEGF‑A and ANGPT2 and thus implicates the angiopoietin/TIE2 axis). Corticosteroids act via the glucocorticoid receptor. Neuropilin‑1 is a VEGF co‑receptor relevant to VEGF signaling. FLT1 and KDR are the VEGF receptor genes present in VEGF‑trap fusion proteins. Based on these drug–target relationships, the genes/proteins associated with drugs that can treat diabetic retinopathy include the following:

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease diffuse astrocytoma.
thinking: Diffuse astrocytoma is primarily treated with alkylating chemotherapies (temozolomide, lomustine/CCNU, carmustine/BCNU, procarbazine), microtubule inhibitors (vincristine), and in some cases anti-VEGF (bevacizumab) or IDH1-directed agents (for IDH1-mutant tumors). Key genes/proteins associated with these drugs are: MGMT (repairs O6-methylguanine, predicts response to alkylators), MMR proteins (MSH6, MSH2, MLH1, PMS2) that mediate temozolomide-induced cytotoxicity and resistance when mutated, PARP1 (base excision repair enzyme that interacts with temozolomide activity and is targeted in combination strategies), TUBB (beta-tubulin, vincristine target), VEGFA (bevacizumab target), and IDH1 (target of IDH1 inhibitors like ivosidenib).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease digitalis poisoning.
thinking: Digitalis (digoxin) toxicity is treated primarily with digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin immune Fab). Supportive and adjunctive drug treatments include atropine for bradycardia, intravenous lidocaine or phenytoin for ventricular arrhythmias, beta-adrenergic agonists (e.g., isoproterenol) for severe bradycardia or heart block, and electrolyte management (potassium/magnesium) which functionally interact with the Na+/K+-ATPase inhibited by digoxin. I listed the principal human gene/protein targets or main molecular effectors associated with those treatments: the Na+/K+-ATPase alpha subunit (target of digoxin and affected by potassium), the cardiac muscarinic M2 receptor (atropine target), cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5 (lidocaine/phenytoin target), beta-adrenergic receptors (isoproterenol targets), and the cardiac L-type calcium channel (affected by electrolyte/ion-channel interactions).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease disorder of phenylalanine metabolism.
thinking: Disorders of phenylalanine metabolism (eg, phenylketonuria/hyperphenylalaninemia) are treated by tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4; sapropterin) which acts on/affects phenylalanine hydroxylase and the BH4 biosynthesis/regeneration pathway, and by enzyme substitution therapy (pegvaliase) which is a phenylalanine ammonia-lyase. I therefore list the gene/protein entities typically associated with these drugs and with phenylalanine metabolism/disease: PAH (the drug target for BH4), the BH4 biosynthesis/regeneration enzymes (GCH1, PTS, SPR, QDPR), the therapeutic enzyme phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL), and DNAJC12 which is implicated in hyperphenylalaninemia and affects PAH function.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease disseminated sporotrichosis.
thinking: Disseminated sporotrichosis is treated primarily with amphotericin B (for severe/disseminated disease) and with oral azoles such as itraconazole for systemic therapy; terbinafine is also used occasionally. I therefore returned genes/proteins known to be associated with those antifungal drugs — fungal drug targets and resistance-associated ERG genes, and major human drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters that interact with these drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease double outlet right ventricle with subaortic or doubly committed ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis.
thinking: Double outlet right ventricle with subaortic (or doubly committed) VSD and pulmonary stenosis is primarily managed surgically, but medical therapies used in preoperative/medical management include prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) to maintain ductal patency in ductal-dependent lesions and supportive drugs for heart-failure or symptomatic management (e.g., digoxin, diuretics such as loop diuretics, and ACE inhibitors or β-blockers when indicated). I therefore list genes/proteins that are known molecular targets or principal metabolizing enzymes associated with those drugs: prostaglandin E (PGE) receptors and metabolism enzymes for alprostadil; Na+/K+-ATPase for digoxin; NKCC2 for loop diuretics; ACE for ACE inhibitors; and β-adrenergic receptors for β-blockers. PTGS1 and PTGS2 (COX enzymes) are included because they are central to prostaglandin synthesis and are commonly annotated in prostaglandin-related drug associations.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease drug-induced osteoporosis.
thinking: I listed genes/proteins that are known targets or key pathway proteins for drugs used to treat osteoporosis (including drug-induced osteoporosis): bisphosphonates (inhibit the mevalonate pathway enzymes), denosumab (anti-RANKL), PTH analogs (act on PTH1R), SERMs and estrogens (estrogen receptors), calcitonin (calcitonin receptor), vitamin D and calcium therapies (VDR, Ca-sensing receptor), anti-sclerostin therapy (romosozumab), and cathepsin K inhibitors. Each listed gene/protein is a standard gene symbol or common protein name corresponding to those drug targets or closely associated pathway proteins.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease dyshidrosis.
thinking: I identified classes of drugs commonly used to treat dyshidrosis (pompholyx) — topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus), systemic therapies used for severe/recalcitrant cases (alitretinoin, cyclosporine, methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate), biologic therapy sometimes used (dupilumab), antihistamines, and botulinum toxin — then listed the principal protein targets or directly associated proteins for those drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease echinococcus granulosus infectious disease.
model_answer: Voltage-dependent (voltage-gated) calcium channel, alpha-1 subunit (CACNA1 family)
Voltage-dependent (voltage-gated) calcium channel, beta subunit (CACNB family)
Transient receptor potential melastatin (TRPM) channels (parasite TRPM_PZQ-like channels)
P-glycoprotein / ATP-binding cassette sub-family B member 1 (ABCB1)
thinking: Echinococcus granulosus (cystic echinococcosis) is primarily treated with benzimidazole anthelmintics (albendazole, mebendazole) whose canonical parasite target is parasite beta-tubulin (microtubule formation). Other drugs used adjunctively (praziquantel) are linked to parasite voltage-gated calcium channels and parasite TRP-type channels; nitazoxanide acts on pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) in anaerobic parasites. Human proteins that affect these drugs’ activation or disposition (and therefore are associated with the drugs) include cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize albendazole (notably CYP3A4) and drug efflux transporters such as P-glycoprotein (ABCB1). I list below the gene/protein entities most directly associated with drugs used to treat Echinococcus granulosus.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease elephantiasis.
thinking: Interpreting “elephantiasis” as lymphatic filariasis (commonly treated with albendazole, ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine and doxycycline), I listed protein/gene entities that are known drug targets or otherwise frequently associated with those antifilarial drugs. For ivermectin I included the parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels (and related nematode gene names) plus known mammalian interaction partners (GABAA subunits, ABCB1). For albendazole I included beta-tubulin (nematode ben-1 / general TUBB). For doxycycline I listed Wolbachia ribosomal proteins and the Wolbachia surface protein (WSP). Diethylcarbamazine’s precise molecular target is not well defined; some literature implicates host/parasite arachidonic-acid/prostaglandin pathways, so I included representative enzymes (ALOX5, PTGS1) as plausible associated proteins. This list aims to capture the main genes/proteins commonly cited in connection with drugs used to treat elephantiasis/lymphatic filariasis.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease embryonal carcinoma of the central nervous system.
thinking: Embryonal carcinoma of the central nervous system is treated with platinum-based and other cytotoxic chemotherapies (e.g., cisplatin/carboplatin, etoposide, bleomycin, ifosfamide/cyclophosphamide, vincristine/paclitaxel, methotrexate). I listed genes/proteins commonly associated as direct drug targets, drug-activating or -metabolizing enzymes, and transporters or DNA-repair proteins that modulate response to these agents (e.g., TOP2A/TOP2B for etoposide; BLMH for bleomycin; SLC31A1, ERCC1, ATP7A/ATP7B for platinum drugs; CYP enzymes for oxazaphosphorine activation; TUBB for microtubule inhibitors; DHFR for methotrexate). These are the likely gene/protein entities linked to drugs used to treat CNS embryonal carcinoma.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease embryonal carcinoma.
thinking: I interpreted the question as asking for genes/proteins that are known targets or are strongly associated (metabolism, activation, or resistance) with drugs used to treat embryonal carcinoma (a testicular germ cell tumor subtype). Common active drugs for embryonal carcinoma include cisplatin, etoposide, bleomycin, paclitaxel, gemcitabine, ifosfamide/cyclophosphamide and related agents; I list proteins that are established drug targets or key metabolizing/repair/resistance factors linked to those drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease endemic goiter.
thinking: Endemic goiter is treated primarily by iodine supplementation (e.g., potassium iodide, iodized salt, Lugol's solution) and by thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine/thyroxine). I listed genes/proteins that are most directly involved in iodide uptake/organification and in thyroid hormone production, transport, activation, and receptor-mediated action — i.e., those most likely to be associated with the drugs used to treat endemic goiter.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease endocrine exophthalmos.
thinking: Endocrine exophthalmos (thyroid eye disease / Graves' ophthalmopathy) is treated with several drugs whose molecular targets are known. Teprotumumab is an approved therapy and targets the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R). Rituximab (used off-label) targets CD20 (gene MS4A1). Tocilizumab (used for refractory cases) targets the interleukin-6 receptor (IL6R). Systemic glucocorticoids such as prednisone act via the glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1). Antithyroid drugs used to treat the underlying Graves disease (methimazole, propylthiouracil) act on thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and propylthiouracil also inhibits deiodinase (DIO1) activity. Mycophenolate mofetil, used as an immunosuppressant in some patients, inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH1/IMPDH2), with IMPDH2 being the predominant immune-cell isoform. The thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) is the central autoantigen in Graves disease and is a target of investigational therapies and is functionally linked to approved therapies (e.g., via the TSHR–IGF1R signaling complex). These genes/proteins therefore are the principal molecular entities associated with drugs that can treat endocrine exophthalmos.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease endocrine pancreas disease.
thinking: I interpreted “endocrine pancreas disease” primarily as disorders of pancreatic endocrine function (most commonly diabetes mellitus) and listed genes/proteins that are known drug targets, receptors, transporters or directly associated proteins for drugs used to treat those conditions (insulin therapies, GLP‑1 receptor agonists, DPP‑4 inhibitors, SGLT inhibitors, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, amylin analogs, alpha‑glucosidase inhibitors, metformin-related proteins, etc.). This is a best-effort comprehensive list of genes/proteins associated with antidiabetic or endocrine‑pancreas–directed drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease enterocolitis .
thinking: Interpretation: “Enterocolitis” can be infectious (e.g., Clostridioides difficile) or inflammatory (eg, IBD-related enterocolitis). I listed proteins/genes that are known targets of drugs used to treat enterocolitis (antibiotics/antitoxins for infectious enterocolitis and biologics/small-molecule/immunomodulator targets for inflammatory enterocolitis). Drugs considered include: vancomycin, fidaxomicin, metronidazole, bezlotoxumab, common antibiotics used for necrotizing enterocolitis (ampicillin, gentamicin, clindamycin, etc.), and anti‑inflammatory/biologic agents used for Crohn’s/colitis (infliximab/adalimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, tofacitinib, corticosteroids). For bacterial drugs I list the bacterial target proteins (and key toxin), for biologics/small molecules I list the human protein targets.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease ependymoblastoma.
thinking: Ependymoblastoma (now classified within ETMR in current WHO CNS tumor taxonomy) is treated primarily with surgery, radiotherapy and cytotoxic chemotherapy. Common chemotherapeutic agents used for embryonal pediatric brain tumors (and reported in ependymoblastoma/ETMR cases or regimens) include vincristine, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, cisplatin/carboplatin, etoposide, methotrexate, temozolomide, irinotecan/topotecan and anthracyclines. I mapped those drugs to their principal molecular targets, metabolizing enzymes or well-known resistance-associated proteins to produce a list of genes/proteins that are associated with drugs that can treat ependymoblastoma. This is a best-effort list based on standard drug-target and drug-metabolism associations; some associations (e.g., DNA repair proteins for platinum drugs) are indirect (repair/detoxification proteins) rather than being direct drug-binding targets.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease epidermodysplasia verruciformis.
thinking: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is treated with several topical and systemic agents (retinoids such as acitretin/isotretinoin/tazarotene, immune modulators such as imiquimod and interferon-α, antivirals such as cidofovir, antimetabolites such as 5‑fluorouracil, and photodynamic therapy agents). I listed the human genes/proteins known to be targets or key signaling/metabolic proteins associated with these drugs: retinoid receptors and binding proteins for acitretin/isotretinoin/tazarotene; TLR/MyD88 pathway and downstream transcription factors for imiquimod; interferon receptors and JAK/STAT signaling components for interferon-α; host kinases and polymerases involved in activation/interaction of cidofovir; thymidylate synthase and 5‑FU catabolic enzymes for 5‑fluorouracil; and enzymes of heme/porphyrin biosynthesis relevant to ALA-based photodynamic therapy. Some associations (e.g., host kinases for cidofovir, host polymerases) are inferred because these drugs act on viral DNA synthesis and require host phosphorylation/metabolism.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease epiglottitis.
thinking: Epiglottitis is most often bacterial and is treated empirically with broad‑spectrum antibiotics (commonly third‑generation cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, aminopenicillins with beta‑lactamase inhibitors such as ampicillin‑sulbactam or amoxicillin‑clavulanate, clindamycin, vancomycin for MRSA coverage, and sometimes trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole). Below I list the main bacterial gene/protein targets associated with those antibiotics (penicillin‑binding proteins are targets of beta‑lactams; clindamycin targets the 50S ribosomal subunit; trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole targets DHFR and DHPS; vancomycin binds the D‑Ala‑D‑Ala peptidoglycan terminus). This is a best‑effort list of the standard gene/protein targets relevant to drugs used to treat epiglottitis.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease epithelioid hemangioendothelioma.
thinking: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) has been treated clinically with mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus/everolimus), anti-VEGF/VEGFR agents (bevacizumab, pazopanib, sorafenib, sunitinib), chemotherapy (doxorubicin, ifosfamide), and occasionally interferons/immune-modulatory drugs. Below I list genes/proteins that are known targets (or are directly bound) by those drugs used to treat EHE. I also include the characteristic EHE fusion proteins (WWTR1–CAMTA1 and YAP1–TFE3), which are disease-associated but are not direct drug targets. Some cytotoxic agents (e.g., ifosfamide) act by DNA alkylation and have no single specific protein target; I have omitted non-specific mechanisms and focused on molecular targets that are typically associated with the listed drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease epithelioid sarcoma.
thinking: Tazemetostat (EZH2 inhibitor) is the approved targeted therapy for advanced epithelioid sarcoma and is prescribed for tumors with loss of SMARCB1 (INI1). Therefore the key genes/proteins associated with a drug that can treat epithelioid sarcoma are EZH2 (the drug target) and SMARCB1/INI1 (the biomarker whose loss defines patients for treatment). Other cytotoxic agents (doxorubicin, ifosfamide, gemcitabine, docetaxel) act on general cellular targets but are not specific biomarkers for epithelioid sarcoma in the same way.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease erythema infectiosum.
thinking: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is caused by Parvovirus B19; no specific antiviral is routinely used, but intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, pooled human IgG) is the established therapy for chronic/parvovirus B19 infections in immunocompromised patients. IVIG contains neutralizing antibodies that target the viral capsid proteins (VP1 and VP2) and antibodies can react with other viral proteins (e.g., NS1). The active therapeutic molecules are immunoglobulin G (IgG) molecules encoded by Ig heavy and light chain genes; IgG effects are mediated through Fc receptors and the neonatal Fc receptor. The list below gives the viral proteins and the main human immunoglobulin genes/proteins and Fc receptors that are most directly associated with the therapeutic action of IVIG in Parvovirus B19 infection.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease erythropoietic protoporphyria.
thinking: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is treated clinically with the α‑MSH analogue afamelanotide (Scenesse) and investigational oral MC1R agonists (e.g. dersimelagon). These drugs are agonists of the melanocortin receptor family, especially melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R). α‑MSH is produced from POMC (proopiomelanocortin) and can act at several melanocortin receptors (MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, MC5R). I include those receptor proteins and the related peptide/hormone. I also list the two genes commonly implicated in EPP (FECH and ALAS2) because they are the disease-associated genes relevant to the therapy context (though they are not direct targets of afamelanotide).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease esophageal cancer.
thinking: I interpreted the question as asking for genes/proteins that are known targets or are clinically associated biomarkers for drugs used to treat esophageal cancer (including cytotoxic chemotherapies, targeted therapies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors). I listed standard gene/protein symbols and, for each, considered typical drugs used in esophageal cancer that target or are linked to that gene/protein (e.g., trastuzumab -> ERBB2; pembrolizumab/nivolumab -> PDCD1; atezolizumab -> CD274; bevacizumab/ramucirumab/VEGFR inhibitors -> VEGFA/KDR; irinotecan -> TOP1; anthracyclines/topoisomerase II inhibitors -> TOP2A; taxanes -> TUBB; 5‑fluorouracil/capecitabine -> TYMS). I also included DNA-repair and mismatch-repair genes (ERCC1, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) that are clinically associated with response to platinum chemotherapy or with eligibility for immunotherapy (MSI-H), and DPYD which is associated with 5‑FU pharmacogenetics. This list focuses on genes/proteins commonly reported in the context of drugs used to treat esophageal cancer.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease esophageal disease.
thinking: Interpretation and approach: “Esophageal disease” is a broad term (includes GERD/peptic esophagitis, eosinophilic esophagitis, achalasia, and esophageal cancer). I listed genes/proteins that are known drug targets of medicines used to treat these esophageal conditions (proton‑pump inhibitors, H2 blockers, prokinetics, GABA‑B agonists, botulinum toxin, topical/systemic steroids and biologics for eosinophilic esophagitis, and targeted/immuno/chemotherapy for esophageal cancer). This is not an exhaustive genome‑wide list but covers the principal molecular targets linked to drugs commonly used to treat esophageal diseases.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease esophageal ulcer.
thinking: Esophageal ulcers are treated by several drug classes (proton‑pump inhibitors, H2‑receptor antagonists, topical corticosteroids for eosinophilic esophagitis, antifungals for Candida, antivirals for CMV, etc.). I listed the genes/proteins that are the known molecular targets or major metabolizing enzymes associated with those drugs: H+/K+ ATPase subunits targeted by PPIs; the histamine H2 receptor targeted by H2 blockers; glucocorticoid receptor for topical steroids; fungal and viral drug targets for antifungals/antivirals; and key cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize PPIs and H2 antagonists (or are inhibited by cimetidine).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease esotropia.
thinking: Esotropia (a form of strabismus) is commonly treated with botulinum neurotoxin (especially botulinum toxin type A). Botulinum toxin proteases cleave SNARE proteins (notably SNAP25 for BoNT/A) and bind synaptic vesicle protein 2 (SV2) isoforms as protein receptors; other SNARE proteins (VAMP/synaptobrevin, syntaxin/STX1A) are targets of other BoNT serotypes and are therefore commonly associated with botulinum drugs used to treat strabismus. Based on these mechanistic associations, the relevant genes/proteins are listed below.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease eumycotic mycetoma.
thinking: Eumycetoma (eumycotic mycetoma) is treated with systemic antifungals (most commonly azoles such as itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole; also terbinafine, amphotericin B and occasionally echinocandins). The principal fungal drug targets and related proteins (and key human metabolizing enzymes and fungal efflux pumps associated with these drugs) are listed below. Mapping: azoles → lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (fungal ERG11 / CYP51), terbinafine → squalene epoxidase (fungal ERG1 / SQLE), echinocandins → 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (FKS1), amphotericin B → ergosterol (ergosterol biosynthesis enzymes such as ERG3, ERG6), and azoles are metabolized by human cytochrome P450s (CYP3A4, CYP2C19, CYP2C9). Fungal ABC and MFS efflux pumps (CDR1, MDR1) are also associated with azole response/resistance.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease exanthema subitum.
thinking: Exanthema subitum (roseola infantum) is usually caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV‑6). Antiviral drugs used for severe HHV‑6 infection include ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir. These drugs act primarily on viral DNA polymerases and, for ganciclovir, require phosphorylation by viral or cellular kinases. Based on known drug targets and activation pathways for these antivirals, the genes/proteins associated with drugs that can treat exanthema subitum include HHV‑6 DNA polymerase (the viral DNA polymerase gene often referred to as U38), the HHV‑6 protein kinase U69 (a viral kinase that can phosphorylate antivirals), the general viral DNA polymerase (Pol), and cellular kinases involved in phosphorylation/activation of nucleoside/nucleotide analog antivirals (notably deoxycytidine kinase and UMP/CMP kinase). I also list CMV UL97 protein kinase because it is the canonical viral kinase associated with ganciclovir activation in related herpesviruses (included because of its relevance to ganciclovir’s mechanism).

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease exercise-induced malignant hyperthermia.
thinking: Exercise-induced malignant hyperthermia is treated primarily with dantrolene (dantrolene sodium/Ryanodex), which acts by inhibiting abnormal calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum via the ryanodine receptor. The principal gene/protein implicated in malignant hyperthermia susceptibility and directly targeted functionally by dantrolene is RYR1. Other genes known to confer MH susceptibility or MH-like, exercise/exertional phenotypes and that are functionally linked to the RYR1-mediated calcium-release pathway (and thus associated with the drug’s mechanism or clinical use) include CACNA1S, STAC3, and CASQ1. Proteins that regulate RYR1 function (and are therefore mechanistically related to dantrolene’s effects) include FKBP1A (FKBP12) and calmodulin (CALM1). Based on these clinical and mechanistic associations, the following gene/protein symbols are listed as the entities associated with the drug used to treat exercise-induced malignant hyperthermia.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease extrinsic allergic alveolitis.
thinking: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) is primarily managed by antigen avoidance and corticosteroids; refractory or progressive fibrosing cases may be treated with immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide), anti-CD20 (rituximab) in selected cases, and antifibrotics (nintedanib, pirfenidone). I listed the molecular targets and key metabolizing enzymes or cytokine mediators that are associated with those drugs: glucocorticoid receptor for corticosteroids; IMPDH, HPRT1 and TPMT/XDH for azathioprine/6‑MP and mycophenolate metabolism/target; MS4A1 (CD20) for rituximab; multiple receptor tyrosine kinases (PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1–3, KDR/VEGFR2, FLT1/VEGFR1, FLT4/VEGFR3) and SRC for nintedanib; and profibrotic/inflammatory mediators (TGFB1, TNF, IL1B, IL6, COL1A1) associated with pirfenidone’s effects. Cyclophosphamide acts by DNA alkylation rather than a specific protein target, so no single protein target is listed for it.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease exudative vitreoretinopathy.
thinking: I interpreted “exudative vitreoretinopathy” as the exudative/vascular form that is treated clinically with intraocular anti-VEGF agents and, in some cases, intraocular corticosteroids. Common drugs used include bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept and pegaptanib (anti-VEGF agents) and corticosteroids such as triamcinolone or dexamethasone implants. The main protein targets of those drugs are VEGF family members and VEGF receptors (for aflibercept, a VEGF-trap composed of VEGFR1/VEGFR2 domains), and the glucocorticoid receptor for steroid drugs. I therefore list the gene/protein entities corresponding to those targets.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease factor VII deficiency.
thinking: Recombinant activated coagulation factor VII (rFVIIa; e.g., NovoSeven) is the drug used to treat factor VII deficiency. rFVIIa acts by binding tissue factor (TF) and directly activating downstream coagulation factors (notably factor X and factor IX); its activity is also modulated by tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI). The genes/proteins most directly associated with the drug are therefore F7 (the administered protein), F3 (tissue factor), F10, F9, and TFPI. Other downstream coagulation components (e.g., F2/thrombin) are involved in the cascade but are less directly associated with the drug’s primary mechanism.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease factor XIII, A subunit, deficiency.
thinking: Congenital factor XIII A-subunit deficiency is treated by factor XIII replacement: recombinant factor XIII A-subunit (catridecacog; brand Tretten) and plasma-derived factor XIII concentrates. The protein provided/replaced by these drugs is the coagulation factor XIII A chain, encoded by F13A1. Plasma-derived concentrates contain the A2B2 heterotetramer and thus include the B subunit encoded by F13B as an associated protein present in the therapeutic product. Therefore the genes/proteins associated with drugs that treat this disease are F13A1 and F13B.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
thinking: I interpreted the question as asking for the gene/protein targets associated with drugs that are used to treat familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). Common medical treatments for symptomatic HCM include beta‑blockers (e.g., metoprolol, propranolol), non‑dihydropyridine calcium‑channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem), the antiarrhythmic disopyramide, and the recently approved cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten. Drugs used for arrhythmias in HCM (e.g., amiodarone) have additional ion-channel targets. I listed the standard gene symbols for the principal protein targets of those drugs.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease familial intrahepatic cholestasis.
thinking: I interpreted the question as asking for gene/protein entities that are known drug targets or are otherwise directly associated with drugs used to treat familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) or to treat cholestatic symptoms in these patients (for example bile-acid transport inhibitors, bile acids, enzyme inducers and drugs used to rescue defective bile salt export). I included proteins that are direct molecular targets of approved PFIC drugs (e.g., IBAT/ASBT inhibitors) and proteins that are mechanistically linked to commonly used pharmacotherapies for PFIC (e.g., BSEP, PXR/rifampicin-mediated induction). This list is not exhaustive of every protein involved in bile-acid physiology, but focuses on genes/proteins that are directly associated with drugs used to treat familial intrahepatic cholestasis or its symptoms.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease familial isolated deficiency of vitamin E.
thinking: Familial isolated vitamin E deficiency (AVED) is treated with high‑dose vitamin E (alpha‑tocopherol). I listed genes/proteins that are known to interact with, transport, metabolize, or regulate vitamin E (alpha‑tocopherol) and so are plausibly associated with the drug used to treat AVED: the alpha‑tocopherol transfer protein (TTPA) is causal for AVED; SEC14L2 encodes an alpha‑tocopherol–binding protein; CYP4F2 (and other CYPs) metabolize tocopherols; SCARB1, NPC1L1, MTTP, ABCA1, APOA1, APOE, and CD36 are involved in intestinal absorption, lipoprotein assembly/transport, or cellular uptake of vitamin E.

question: Name all gene/proteins that are associated with drug that can treat disease familial thrombocytosis.
thinking: Familial (hereditary) thrombocytosis is managed with platelet-lowering or antithrombotic drugs such as cytoreductive agents (hydroxyurea), anagrelide, interferon-alpha, low‑dose aspirin, and (when indicated) JAK inhibitors (e.g., ruxolitinib).
